CHAPTER I

The lamp had gone out an hour before she noticed. Margaret sat very still at the writing desk, her pen dry, the letter unfinished before her. Outside, the elm trees moved in a way that seemed almost deliberate, as if they were trying to attract her attention. She had been in this house for three weeks now, long enough to know its sounds and silences, its drafts and warm pockets, the particular creak of the third stair. What she had not learned was how to be alone in it without feeling that the house itself was watching her, forming judgments she would never be permitted to hear. She rose, went to the window, and pressed her forehead against the cold glass. The garden below was dark and still, and she could not say why this surprised her, only that it did, and that the surprise felt like a reminder of something she had been trying not to think about.

She had known James for eleven years before she understood that his silences were not merely a habit of reserve but a form of argument — a way of declining to be wrong by declining to speak at all. In the early years of their acquaintance she had taken this quality for depth, for a seriousness of character that set him apart from the men she had known before, who filled every available silence with opinions they had not thought through and could not have defended. James never offered an opinion he could not defend. The difficulty was that he applied this standard to feelings as well, and feelings, as Margaret had come to understand, rarely survived the process of making themselves defensible. She remembered the evening he had held her hand in the park and said nothing for a long time, and how she had believed for many years afterward that this silence meant more than any words could have managed. It was only later that she began to wonder whether it had simply meant less, or whether she had invented the meaning herself and then forgotten she had done so.

The question of the letters had been settled between them years ago, or so she had believed when they agreed to settle it. They were to be destroyed — the ones from the first year specifically. Not because there was anything in them that either party needed to be ashamed of, but because they belonged to a version of the friendship that no longer existed, and keeping them would be like preserving a pressed flower from a garden that had since been cleared and built over entirely. She had agreed to this without reservation, or nearly without reservation, and the distinction had not seemed important at the time. She had kept three of the letters. Not for any reason she could articulate clearly even to herself, except that they seemed to contain a quality of attention she had not encountered again in the years since — something she still could not name with any precision, only recognize when she came across it, the way you recognize a particular quality of light in a room you have not visited for a very long time. She was afraid that destroying the paper would destroy also the faint impression it had left in her memory, the way a seal pressed into warm wax leaves its mark even after the seal itself is lifted and carried away.

It had been her grandmother's house first, and before that her grandmother's grandmother's, and the weight of this succession was something Margaret had not anticipated when she agreed to take it on — not a burden exactly, more a kind of pressure, evenly distributed, the way water exerts pressure at depth without seeming to push from any particular direction. She had expected to feel the history of the place as something grand, or at least as something legible, a series of lives she could read in the furniture and the portraits and the particular arrangement of rooms. What she found instead was that the history was too intimate to be read that way, that it pressed itself into the texture of ordinary things — the worn patch on the third stair where four generations of hands had gripped the banister, the slight unevenness of the kitchen floor where the house had settled, over decades, toward the east — and that living inside it required a constant negotiation she had not known how to name until she tried to describe it to her sister on the telephone one evening, and heard herself say, without having planned to say it, that she felt like a guest who had been given the master bedroom and could not quite convince herself she had the right to rearrange the furniture. Her sister had laughed and said she was being dramatic, and perhaps she was. But the feeling did not go away, and she had begun to wonder whether the right response to it was to resist it or to find some way to make peace with it, to accept that certain inheritances came with conditions she had not been given the opportunity to negotiate in advance, and that accepting them did not mean she had agreed to them, only that she had decided to live inside them, which was a different thing, though the difference was not always visible from outside.

There was a morning early in the second winter when she had walked out onto the frozen lake alone, without telling anyone where she was going, which was itself a kind of statement she had found herself unable to make in any other form available to her at that particular time in her life. The ice was three inches thick, the estate manager had confirmed when she asked him carefully, quite safe for a person of ordinary weight. She walked to the center of the lake, which took considerably longer than she had expected — the far shore remaining stubbornly at the same apparent distance no matter how many steps she took in its direction — and she stood there in the middle for a period of time she later could not measure with any confidence. The cold was not uncomfortable, or at least it was not uncomfortable in any way she felt she needed to resist. The sky was the particular white of winter mornings that seems to contain light without releasing it, a quality she came to associate thereafter with a certain kind of suspension, the feeling of a moment that has not yet decided what it intends to become. When she finally turned around to begin the walk back to the house, it looked smaller than she remembered it, and for a full minute she stood looking at it, memorizing this particular version of it — the one that distance and cold and the angle of the winter light had made together — before it became necessary to return and become again the person the house expected her to be.
